column15: Source reports a mean absolute percentage error of about 1%. Converted to a standard deviation assuming the replicate deviations are normally distributed with zero mean, so SD = MAE * sqrt(pi/2) = MAE * 1.2533, giving CV = 1.25%. If the replicate error is heavier-tailed than normal this UNDERSTATES the SD. Left in relative units; no absolute SD is given because analytical error scales with SOC concentration, not with stock.
column19: Understates on two independent counts. (1) The MAE-to-SD conversion assumes normality; replicate errors with heavier tails would give a larger SD (D-003). (2) More importantly, the source quantified this from two technical replicates of the SAME milled aliquot, which excludes subsampling and sample-preparation error entirely. VC-ANA-004 shows processing error can dwarf instrument error, so 1% is the narrowest possible slice of 'analytical error'.

column4: Between-plot spatial variability of SOC CONCENTRATION, as the within-treatment within-site residual CV among replicate experimental units under identical management.
column15: DERIVED BY US from the primary dataset; see scripts/derive_g1_napeshm.py. Replicate EUs under identical management at one site differ only by spatial heterogeneity plus analytical error, so their residual variance is between-plot spatial variance. Estimated as the residual of a REML nested random-effects model, treatment nested within site, NOT by averaging per-treatment variances (unstable at 2-6 replicates, and it would weight a 2-replicate treatment equally with a 6-replicate one). Fitted on the LOG scale because within-treatment SD scales with treatment mean (log-log slope about 1.2, far from the 0 a constant-SD model assumes), so the natural parameter is a constant CV; CV = 100*sqrt(exp(sigma^2)-1). The interval is a 95% cluster bootstrap over SITES, the top-level independent unit - bootstrapping rows or treatments would ignore the nesting and give far too narrow an interval. 600/600 resamples converged and the bootstrap median (11.8%) sits essentially on the point estimate, so the estimator shows no material bias.
column19: UPPER BOUND, not a point estimate. NAPESHM has no lab duplicate, split-sample or QC columns, so analytical error cannot be separated from spatial error and the residual necessarily contains both (D-027). Since variances add, the true between-plot SPATIAL term is strictly smaller than 11.9%. Using VC-ANA-001's 1.25% analytical CV as a rough guide, the purely spatial part would be near sqrt(11.9^2 - 1.25^2) = 11.8% - so the inflation is small, but it is one-directional and must not be forgotten when this row feeds the Phase 5 audit (D-023).

column4: Between-plot spatial variability of SOC STOCK at 0-15 cm, as the within-treatment within-site residual CV among replicate experimental units under identical management.
column15: Same estimator, dataset and filters as VC-BPS-005; see scripts/derive_g1_napeshm.py. Stock computed per EU as b_soc/100 * bd_2mm * 15 * 100 = b_soc * bd_2mm * 15 Mg C/ha, so bulk density measurement error is propagated into this row and VC-BPS-005 is the cleaner of the two. sd_mg_c_ha = 11.5% * 24.99 = 2.86 Mg C/ha using the mean 0-15 cm stock of the SAME 372 EUs, so the reference stock is internal to the data rather than assumed by us - but the row is still flagged mean_dependent because the absolute figure moves if that mean is revised. COUNTER-INTUITIVE RESULT, DELIBERATELY NOT SUPPRESSED: stock CV (11.5%) is LOWER than concentration CV (11.9%) even though stock carries the extra bulk-density error. The cause is a within-treatment correlation between log SOC and log bulk density of -0.280: plots richer in organic matter are less dense, and at FIXED DEPTH the two partly cancel in the stock product. The negative covariance term (2*cov = -0.00179) outweighs the added density variance (+0.00109). This is a property of the fixed-depth convention, not a property of the soil. RE-DERIVED under D-028's IPCC scope. The effect SURVIVES the scope change but WEAKENS: the correlation moves -0.396 -> -0.280 and the gap between the two rows narrows from 1.0 to 0.5 percentage points. Worth watching - it is the same mechanism that biases fixed-depth stock CHANGE (VC-BDC-001/002), and its magnitude is evidently scope-dependent rather than a constant of the soil.
column19: Upper bound for the same reason as VC-BPS-005 - analytical error is not separable from spatial error in this dataset (D-027) - and here bulk density measurement error is folded in as well, so the residual contains three sources where we want one. column15: DERIVED BY US (D-041, D-046). The plot term of the crossed model log C ~ treatment + (1|plot) + (1|occasion), fitted per site on the Wuest & Durfee monthly series. Because each plot is measured on 39 separate occasions, within-plot spatial and analytical error land in the residual and NOT in this term - repeated visits average them out of the plot mean. That is what makes this row different in kind from VC-BPS-005/006, which are single-visit and therefore combined. CV = 100*sqrt(exp(sigma^2)-1) (D-029); 95% block bootstrap over occasions. No absolute SD is published: the layer is 0-30 cm, six 5-cm increments and an SD in Mg C/ha would invite addition into a 0-30 cm budget (D-042).
column19: No direction can be defended, and for once that is a statement about the estimand rather than about ignorance. The usual inflation - within-plot spatial and analytical error riding along - is genuinely absent here, which is the whole point of the row. What remains is a transfer question: these are long-established research plots on deliberately uniform fields, 3.6-9 m wide, which would push the term DOWN relative to a working farm field; but they are also dryland silt loams with a fallow phase, and whether that pushes plot-to-plot heterogeneity up or down against irrigated or humid cropland is not something we can sign (D-023).

column15: DERIVED BY US from the monthly series, not read from the paper (D-041). Crossed random effects on log SOC stock, plot and sampling occasion, with the treatment as a fixed effect so the plot term means "between replicate experimental units" and not "between treatments": log C ~ treatment + (1|plot) + (1|occasion). Occasion is the sampling CAMPAIGN, not the calendar date - four Adams campaigns ran across two consecutive days and keying on date would split those months into half-occasions and manufacture an occasion effect. This row is the occasion component PLUS the residual: what a single plot revisited on a new date actually shows. The residual is plot x occasion interaction, within-plot spatial variability at the new core position, and analytical error, and this design cannot split them - one measurement per plot per occasion. CV = 100*sqrt(exp(sigma^2)-1), the same convention as D-029. Estimated by closed-form ANOVA moments for a balanced two-way crossed design, which is exact here; REML agrees to within 0.53 CV points across all five series. The interval is a 95% block bootstrap over OCCASIONS - the independent unit along time. Plots are fixed by design and resampling them would answer a different question. NO absolute SD is published for this row on purpose. The layer is top 250 kg/m2 of dry soil, about 20 cm, and an SD in Mg C/ha would invite being added to a 0-30 cm budget, which is the cross-depth rescaling D-042 forbids.
column19: Contains within-plot spatial variability and analytical error as well as temporal variation, and cannot separate them, so it is strictly an upper bound on the temporal term (D-043). column15: TWO assumptions, both consequential. (1) NORMALITY: the source reports mean absolute error, defined in its Eq. 3 as the mean of |SOC_initial - SOC_resampled| across sites. Assuming those paired differences are normal with zero mean, SD = MAE * sqrt(pi/2) = 5.1 * 1.2533 = 6.39 Mg C/ha, and likewise 7.5% -> 9.4%. (2) DIFFERENCE SCALE: 6.39 is the SD of the DIFFERENCE between two locations, not of a single observation. If the two locations are treated as independent draws from the same field, the per-observation relocation SD is 6.39 / sqrt(2) = 4.52 Mg C/ha. Phase 1 must state which of the two it is using; conflating them inflates or deflates MDC by a factor of sqrt(2). Not marked mean_dependent because the source reports both absolute and relative forms directly, so no assumed mean stock was needed.
column19: Understates realistic resampling error.
